title: Butte Valley Formation, facies c (limestone-mudstone facies)
description: Fine to medium-grained carbonates and mudstones, without the coarse clastic rocks in the other facies (Cole, 1986). Thermal metamorphism effects are weak but ubiquitous. This unit is 265 m thick (Cole, 1986).

title: Butte Valley Formation, facies d  (mudstone-quartzite-limestone facies)
description: Abundant calcareous silty mudstone and calcareous quartzite, with minor limestone beds in the upper portions (Cole, 1986). Thermal metamorphism is weak but ubiquitous. A 13 m thick limestone bed occurs near the top of the unit, which contains gastropods that are not preserved well enough for identification. This unit is 340 m thick.

title: Bonanza King Formation
description: Massive bluish gray carbonate angular clasts exposed in a small remnant breccia deposit on the ridge between Butte Valley and Middle Park. Correlated to Bonanza King Formation (Cichanski, 1995) based on the massive blue-gray carbonate of the clasts and of nearby breccia deposits of Stirling Quartzite. The Bonanza King Formation is the next stratigraphic unit upwards with thick-bedded non-fossiliferous carbonates.

title: Lost Burro Formation
description: 40 m of massive yellowish to gray dolomite correlated to the Lost Burro Formation (Wrucke et al., 2008). Wrucke and Stevens (1998) interpreted a moderately north dipping reverse fault to emplace the Lost Burro Formation over the Tin Mountain Limestone but this study found no evidence for such a fault and instead found low rake fault striae on the fault surfaces along the contact with the quartz diorite of Tram Canyon.

title: diorite
description: Porphyritic dikes of plagioclase phenocrysts within dark green fine-grained matrix. These define a west-northwest trending, 1–2 km wide, 9 km long dike swarm along the Middle Park-South Park Canyons divide. These correlate with the regionally observed Independence dike swarm, seen farther west in the Argus and Inyo Mountains and farther south in the Mojave Desert. The dike swarm in the Panamint Range ends to the west at the Goldbug fault zone, but similar dikes were observed within the quartz feldspar gneiss. These dikes have abundant chlorite and epidote mineralization due to Cretaceous retrograde metamorphism. Similar dikes in Redlands Canyon are cut by the Manly Peak quartz monzonite. Three of these dikes were dated via zircon TIMS U-Pb with ages of ~148 Ma (Andrew, 2002).

title: ids
description: White fine-grained catclasite occurs as sheets within the hanging wall breccia of the Emigrant fault in Surprise Canyon (also discussed in the Miocene breccias above). Zircon LA-ICPMS analysis yielded Early Jurassic ages with a weighted mean 206Pb/238U age of 173.38 ± 0.65 Ma. Three concordant CA-TIMS zircon 206Pb(Th-corrected)/238U fractions gave an age of 178.27 ± 0.43 Ma, the rest were discordant with significant inheritance of Proterozoic basement zircon cores (Andrew, unpublished data). This age is similar to the Hunter Mountain Quartz Monzonite, which is interpreted to palinspastically restore to above this area at about 11 Ma (Andrew and Walker, 2009). A potential related body of this rock is a small granitic pluton exposed eastward in Surprise Canyon in the footwall of the Emigrant fault that has an age of 175.6 ± 3.2 Ma (Subia, 2019).

title: hornblende diorite of Goler Wash, <Null>
description: Medium-grained granodiorite dikes and small stocks that intrude the Proterozoic strata in eastern Anvil Spring Canyon. These may be related to the Manly Peak Quartz Monzonite.

title: hornblende diorite of Goler Wash
description: Hornblende diorite that occurs within quartz-feldspar gneiss along the western flank of the Panamint Range. Retrograde metamorphism with chlorite mineralization is abundant. A sample from Goler Wash has a CA-TIMS zircon 206Pb(Th-corrected)/238U age of 177.721 ± 0.074 Ma (Andrew, 2019). The westernmost and structurally highest exposures of this unit have strong ductile fabrics with top-to-the-northeast relative shear, similar to the Jurassic East Sierran thrust system, found in the nearby southern Slate and Argus Ranges (Dunne and Walker, 2004).

title: ids
description: Porphyritic dikes of plagioclase phenocrysts within dark green fine-grained matrix. These define a west-northwest trending, 1–2 km wide, 9 km long dike swarm along the Middle Park-South Park Canyons divide. These correlate with the regionally observed Independence dike swarm, seen farther west in the Argus and Inyo Mountains and farther south in the Mojave Desert. The dike swarm in the Panamint Range ends to the west at the Goldbug fault zone, but similar dikes were observed within the quartz feldspar gneiss. These dikes have abundant chlorite and epidote mineralization due to Cretaceous retrograde metamorphism. Similar dikes in Redlands Canyon are cut by the Manly Peak quartz monzonite. Three of these dikes were dated via zircon TIMS U-Pb with ages of ~148 Ma (Andrew, 2002).

title: quartz diorite of Tram Canyon
description: Medium-grained porphyritic quartz diorite with coarser plagioclase crystals within a fine dark gray silicic matrix. CA-TIMS zircon 206Pb(Th-corrected)/238U age of 151.23 ± 0.13 (Andrew, 2019). Previous geochronologic work determined ages of 154 Ma (Recalculated K-Ar: Stevens et al., 1974) and 139.5 ± 1.3 Ma (TIMS U-Pb zircon: Andrew, 2002). Biotite and hornblende from this unit yielded K-Ar ages of 154.7 ± 5 and 147.1 ± 5 Ma, respectively (Wrucke et al., 2008). Wrucke et al. (2008) refers to this unit as a tonalite. This units contains many 1–12 m inclusions of the wall rocks exposed to the north.

title: rhyolitic dike
description: West-northwest trending dike of light-colored tuffaceous rock that cuts folded Warm Spring Canyon Formation north of Anvil Spring Canyon. This rock is possibly an along-strike continuation of the dike swarm exposedto the west.

title: Warm Spring Canyon Formation, andesite flow meta-breccia
description: Breccia of clasts of dominantly andesite with lesser rhyolite in a dark gray aphanitic matrix (Cole, 1986). There is one lenticular sandstone within this. The total thickness is 367 m. A rhyolitic tuff protolith from the lower portion of this unit has a U-Pb age of 154 ± 7 Ma (Dunne et al., 1998).

title: Warm Spring Canyon Formation, limestone meta-breccia
description: Cream to gray colored, generally tabular clasts of limestone in a very fine-grained dark gray clay matrix (Cole, 1986). Bedding is distinct, as thin to medium thicknesses that are gradational but generally fining upward. Other clasts observed are gneiss cobbles and hornblende meta-andesite clasts. The thickness varies (4.5–49 m thick) and its thickness pattern is lenticular as a whole. Jg LEUCOGRANITE (Early Jurassic(?)) – A few small leucogranite bodies are exposed along the basement gneiss-Crystal Spring contact in central Surprise Canyon. These appear to intrude the contact and Crystal Spring Formation implying they are not Proterozoic in age. These small bodies may correlate to the cataclastic leucogranite discussed below. Subia (2019) dated one of these bodies using zircon U-Pb zircon LA-ICPMS at 175.6 ± 3.2 Ma.

title: Warm Spring Canyon Formation
description: Defined by Johnson (1957) and modified by Wrucke (1966). It is intruded by slightly younger Manly Peak Quartz Monzonite and cut by a dike associated with Late Jurassic Independence dike swarm (Andrew, 2002). Andrew (2002) inferred this formation to be the co-magmatic volcanic rocks to the Independence dike swarm.

title: Warm Spring Canyon Formation, flow-banded meta-andesites
description: This unit is composed of flow-banded hornfels-facies meta-andesites, with two levels of flow breccias (Cole, 1986). This is 182 m thick.

title: Warm Spring Canyon Formation, porphyritic meta-andesite
description: Massive meta-andesite, locally banded and also brecciated (Cole, 1986). Plagioclase phenocrysts are conspicuous throughout these exposures. This unit is locally sheared along its northernmost exposures in Warm Spring Canyon, and it is locally in fault contact with Permian rock units. There is a small lenticular carbonate body in one of the northern exposures, which is nonconformable to the flows. The thickness is at least 788 m, but the upper contact is not exposed.

title: Warm Spring Canyon Formation
description: Defined by Johnson (1957) and modified by Wrucke (1966). It is intruded by slightly younger Manly Peak Quartz Monzonite and cut by a dike associated with Late Jurassic Independence dike swarm (Andrew, 2002). Andrew (2002) inferred this formation to be the co-magmatic volcanic rocks to the Independence dike swarm.

title: Warm Spring Canyon Formation, metaignimbrite tuff
description: This rock contains light-gray angular to lens-shaped fragments that are similar to flattened lapilli. This is up to 30 m thick in Warm Spring Canyon and is missing in the southwestern exposures. A sample of this was dated by Andrew (2002) with an interpreted age of 148 Ma. The same sample analyzed using modern techniques yielded CA-TIMS zircon 206Pb(Th-corrected)/238U age of 151.88 ± 0.15 Ma (Andrew, 2019).

title: Hall Canyon granite
description: Medium-grained leucocratic granite consisting of sodic plagioclase, quartz, microcline, and muscovite; locally, a minor amount of biotite and a trace of garnet are observed (Labotka et al., 1980). The main part of the intrusion occurs in western Hall and Jail Canyons, just north of the map area, but there are smaller exposures in Surprise Canyon. The crystallization age is interpreted to be 72.7 ± 0.6 Ma from Rb/Sr isochron analysis (Mahood et al., 1996). Local strong foliation fabrics occur in this granite, related folds indicate top-west shear under ductile conditions.

title: Manly Peak quartz monozite
description: Medium-grained, massive quartz monzonite with large phenocrysts of pink microcline and roughly equal amounts of biotite and hornblende mafic accessory minerals (Johnson, 1957). A sample of this unit has a CA-TIMS zircon 206 Pb(Th-corrected)/238U age of 151.210 ± 0.074 Ma (Andrew, 2019). Previous studies determined earliest Cretaceous ages of 142–145 Ma: recalculated K-Ar (Armstrong and Suppe, 1973); hornblende K-Ar (Wrucke et al., 2008); and U-Pb zircon TIMS (McKenna et al., 1993; Andrew, 2002).

title: granodoritic gneiss of Pleasant Canyon
description: Medium-grained granodiorite dikes and small stocks that intrude the Proterozoic strata in eastern Anvil Spring Canyon. These may be related to the Manly Peak Quartz Monzonite.

title: granite of Redlands Canyon
description: Garnet-bearing leucocratic alkali granite, that resembles the Late Cretaceous Hall Canyon and Skidoo Granites also occur along the western flank of the Panamint Range. This rock contains several percent of a fine-sized garnet phenocrysts. TIMS zircon U-Pb age of ~91.8 Ma (Andrew, 2002).

title: South Park Canyon granodiorite
description: A porphyritic to medium-grained granodiorite. The eastern edge is locally deformed by top-east reverse faults with local augen gneissic textures. Several dextral strike-slip, ductile shear zones deform this pluton. The TIMS U-Pb zircon age of this unit is 107 ± 1 Ma (Cichanski, 1995).

title: Indian Springs Formation
description: Predominantly brown-weathering siltstone and shale with minor crinoidal limestone. The thickness is 6 m in Warm Spring Canyon (Wrucke et al., 2008).

title: Stone Canyon Formation
description: Thinly interbedded dark-gray, cherty limestone, chert and silicified micrite. Distinguished by the brownish color of weathered outcrops and the fine alternation of these different rock types (Stevens et al., 1996). In Warm Spring Canyon this formation is 75 m thick (Wrucke et al., 2008).

title: Santa Rosa Formation
description: Massive, light-gray, echinodermal limestone with minor amounts of chert (Stone et al., 1989). Thickness in Warm Spring Canyon is ~200 m (Wrucke et al., 2008).

title: Tin Mountain Limestone
description: Medium to dark-gray, thin to medium bedded, fine-grained limestone containing gray to black chert lenses and nodules (Stone et al., 1989). The thickness in Warm Spring Canyon is ~40 m thick (Wrucke et al., 2008).

title: older conglomerate
description: The oldest conglomerate found along the western flank of the Panamint Range is strongly deformed and tilted and is in fault contact with an underlying low-angle fault gouge zone. Strong calcite and silica cementation is notable in this unit. The strongly cemented and deformed conglomerates have tilts similar to those of Miocene volcanic and sedimentary rocks in the Argus and Slate Ranges and for units in the Nova Formation in the northern Panamint Range (Hodges et al., 1990; Snyder and Hodges, 2000). The clast types are predominantly the same as the local bedrock, mostly quartz feldspar gneiss and diabase.

title: Emigrant gouge
description: Areas of gouge developed on the Emigrant fault, which bounds the footwall rocks of the Panamint Range (Andrew and Walker, 2009). This fault dips gently westward and has top-to-the-west northwest movement. This gouge is up to 0.6 m thick and contains S-C fabrics, extensional shear bands, sigma clasts, and strong oxidation. Synthetic and antithetic faults in the hanging wall terminate into the gouge. The gouge is observed to shear and incorporate the older, well-cemented conglomerate unit, but not the younger conglomerate.

title: younger conglomerate
description: Coarse clastic rocks along the western Panamint Range front that overlie an older well-cemented and tilted conglomerate with a prominent angular unconformity. These intermediate age coarse clastic rocks have low eastward to horizontal dips and are poorly cemented. This unit was deposited directly onto the range-bounding fault surface, fault gouge, and the older strongly deformed sediments. Younger uncemented coarse clastic material from alluvial fans overlies these conglomerates. These intermediate units are cut by numerous high-angle faults and local clastic dikes, and are only strongly tilted and deformed within a few meters of faults. Faults cutting these intermediate age units range from normal to strike slip and were not observed to cut the underlying detachment fault (Andrew and walker, 2009). Near the ghost town of Ballarat, a reworked ash layer correlative with the Bishop Tuff (U-Pb zircon ages ~760 ka old; Vogel et al., 2002) occurs within a thick section (>100 m) of coarse sediments that are deeply incised and unconformably overlie strongly deformed, well-cemented coarse sediments in fault contact with fault gouge. Thus, these intermediate-age sediments are in part as young as Pleistocene, while the strongly deformed sediments on the gouge zone are significantly older.

title: Bird Spring Formation
description: Light gray to white limestones alternating with dark gray limestones in beds 40–200 cm thick. Cherty beds and nodules in the middle of the section, and shales and argillaceous limestones near the top. Fossiliferous throughout (Johnson, 1957). The middle 970 m are exposed at Striped Butte, and the lower 200 m and upper 700 m are exposed in Warm Spring Canyon (Stone, 1984). Low-grade metamorphism affected these rocks in Warm Spring Canyon, but not at Striped Butte (Stone, 1984).

title: Owens Valley Formation, lower member
description: Thick bedded dolomite and sandy dolomite interbedded with quartzite and dolomitic quartzite and overlain by dark-reddish-brown-weathering quartzite and pelite (Albee et al., 1981). 150–330 m thick (Labotka et al., 1980).

title: Owens Valley Formation, upper member
description: Thinly laminated micaceous green argillite with rare sandy dolomite and limestone layers changing upward into gray argillite and gray-green silty limestone. Quartzite beds increase near the top. This member is 400–650 m thick (Labotka et al., 1980).

title: alluvium
description: Unconsolidated silt, sand, and gravel deposited in now-abandoned stream channels. These deposits have poor soil and desert varnish development and are not incised.

title: colluvium
description: Poorly sorted, unconsolidated angular debris of local derivation deposited on slopes.

title: eolian
description: Well-sorted, unconsolidated silt or sand deposited in dunes and dune fields.

title: Noonday Dolomite, Mahagony Flat Member
description: 125–150 m of thick-bedded to massive light-gray dolomite with minor thin argillite beds near the top. This unit was originally mapped in the map area as the Redlands Member by Johnson (1957) but renamed and redefined by Petterson et al. (2011).

title: younger intermediate age alluvial
description: Unconsolidated silt, sand, and gravel deposited in now-abandoned stream channels. These deposits have poor soil and desert varnish development and are not incised.

title: older intermediate age alluvial
description: Unconsolidated silt, sand, and gravel deposits with moderate development of desert pavement and desert varnish. Commonly occur as slightly upraised terraces above active and young inactive alluvium. These deposits are younger than local Pleistocene lakes and so do not have lacustrine effects.

title: older intermediate age alluvial
description: Unconsolidated silt, sand, and gravel deposits with moderate development of desert pavement and desert varnish. Commonly occur as slightly upraised terraces above active and young inactive alluvium. These deposits are younger than local Pleistocene lakes and so do not have lacustrine effects.

title: pluvial
description: Well-sorted, unconsolidated silt and clay deposited in active playa lakes. This unit includes playas in the high plateau between Pleasant and Redlands Canyons. These plateau playas have been interpreted to be remnants of uplifted and eastward back-tilted stream valleys (Maxson, 1950).

title: older alluvial
description: Dissected alluvium and fanglomerates that have well-developed pavement surfaces.

title: older lake sediments
description: Gravel deposits along the margins of the Panamint Range with evidence of wave action along paleo-shorelines during high-stand paleo-lakes, such as rounded clasts and tufa deposits.

title: washed surface
description: Older sediments with surfaces modified by Pleistocene Panamint and Searles Lakes. These washed surfaces consist of numerous paleo-lake shoreline beaches and wave-cut terraces. The uppermost washed area is bound by the high-stand at 664 m elevation in Panamint Valley (Smith, 1977). These washed surfaces correlate with members A to B of the Searles Lake Formation (Smith, 2009).

title: Noonday Dolomite
description: Dominantly dolomite and dolomitic limestone, extensively metamorphosed adjacent to the Manly Peak quartz monzonite. Exposures on the western range flank are locally strongly brecciated and displaced down slope by extensional faulting or mass wasting. These rocks weather to a distinctive light-yellow color visible from a distance. Age interpreted from Macdonald et al. (2013).

title: Warm Spring canyon older fanglomerate
description: Weakly cemented alluvial deposits now preserved on ridges and slopes 10s–100s of meters above active alluvial channels in the Warm Spring Canyon area. The best exposure of this is a coarse fanglomerate on the ridge northeast of Warm Spring Canyon that overlaps a small exposure of eroded Miocene volcanic rocks, which overlie the Warm Spring Canyon fault (Andrew, 2019). This exposure contains conspicuous boulder-sized subangular quartzite clasts. Previous workers interpreted this fault to be an intrusive contact (Wrucke, 1966; Wrucke et al., 2008). Npc OLDER CONGLOMERATE (Pliocene) – The oldest conglomerate found along the western flank of the Panamint Range is strongly deformed and tilted and is in fault contact with an underlying low-angle fault gouge zone. Strong calcite and silica cementation is notable in this unit. The strongly cemented and deformed conglomerates have tilts similar to those of Miocene volcanic and sedimentary rocks in the Argus and Slate Ranges and for units in the Nova Formation in the northern Panamint Range (Hodges et al., 1990; Snyder and Hodges, 2000). The clast types are predominantly the same as the local bedrock, mostly quartz feldspar gneiss and diabase.

title: Little Chief granite
description: Rapakivi textured granitic porphyry with CA-TIMS zircon weighted mean 206Pb(Th-corrected)/238U age of 11.460 ± 0.023 Ma (Andrew, 2018). The map area only includes the southern intrusive phase, which has 5% mafic minerals of hornblende and biotite or just biotite with zoned plagioclase and unzoned sanidine in a fine-grained groundmass of quartz. A younger phase of intrusion, exposed just north of the map area, is distinguished by 10% mafic minerals (McDowell, 1974; Albee et al., 1981). The younger phase has a CA-TIMS zircon weighted mean 206Pb(Th-corrected)/238U age of 11.302 ± 0.026 Ma (Andrew, 2018). Nmp FELSIC PYROCLASTIC DEPOSIT (Miocene) – This unit is a conspicuous white tuffaceous bed within the otherwise dark-colored basaltic-andesite lava flow sequence interbedded in the Miocene volcanic section in Anvil Spring Canyon. The exposures in Warm Spring and Anvil Canyons are generally reworked tuffaceous deposits.

title: eastern Panamint fanglomerate
description: Poorly cemented sand and gravel deposits deposited along the eastern Panamint Range, seen in the eastern Warm Spring and Anvil Spring Canyons in the map area. Clast size ranges from pebble to boulder in size. This sediment appears to be locally derived from the bedrock of the eastern Panamint Range.

title: andesite
description: A sequence of basaltic-andesite lava flows with lesser amounts of basalt and andesite lava. This lava sequence is a stack of numerous 3-7 m thick lava flows of basaltic-andesite. This basaltic-andesite lava and the tuff assemblage correlates to the ~14 Ma volcanic sequences in the southern Panamint Range, Slate Range, and Owlshead Mountains (Wagner and Hsu, 1988; Luckow et al., 2005; Andrew and Walker, 2009). A latite flow near Warm Spring Canyon yielded a 40Ar/39Ar age from hornblende of 13.56 ± 0.82 Ma, and an overlying tuff gave a zircon fission-track age of 10.3 ± 0.5 Ma (Topping, 1993). The area south of Anvil Spring Canyon is interpreted by Wagner and Hsu (1988) as a large volcanic edifice. Related volcanic rocks in the Wingate Wash–Owlshead Mountains, southern Panamint Range, and Slate Range, yield 40Ar/39Ar ages of 12.1–14 Ma (Wagner and Hsu, 1988; Luckow et al., 2005; Andrew and Walker, 2009).

title: andesite
description: A sequence of basaltic-andesite lava flows with lesser amounts of basalt and andesite lava. This lava sequence is a stack of numerous 3-7 m thick lava flows of basaltic-andesite. This basaltic-andesite lava and the tuff assemblage correlates to the ~14 Ma volcanic sequences in the southern Panamint Range, Slate Range, and Owlshead Mountains (Wagner and Hsu, 1988; Luckow et al., 2005; Andrew and Walker, 2009). A latite flow near Warm Spring Canyon yielded a 40Ar/39Ar age from hornblende of 13.56 ± 0.82 Ma, and an overlying tuff gave a zircon fission-track age of 10.3 ± 0.5 Ma (Topping, 1993). Related volcanic rocks in the Wingate Wash–Owlshead Mountains, southern Panamint Range, and Slate Range, yield 40Ar/39Ar ages of 12.1–14 Ma (Wagner and Hsu, 1988; Luckow et al., 2005; Andrew and Walker, 2009).

title: andesite
description: A sequence of basaltic-andesite lava flows with lesser amounts of basalt and andesite lava. This lava sequence is a stack of numerous 3-7 m thick lava flows of basaltic-andesite. This basaltic-andesite lava and the tuff assemblage correlates to the ~14 Ma volcanic sequences in the southern Panamint Range, Slate Range, and Owlshead Mountains (Wagner and Hsu, 1988; Luckow et al., 2005; Andrew and Walker, 2009). A latite flow near Warm Spring Canyon yielded a 40Ar/39Ar age from hornblende of 13.56 ± 0.82 Ma, and an overlying tuff gave a zircon fission-track age of 10.3 ± 0.5 Ma (Topping, 1993). The area south of Anvil Spring Canyon is interpreted by Wagner and Hsu (1988) as a large volcanic edifice. Related volcanic rocks in the Wingate Wash–Owlshead Mountains, southern Panamint Range, and Slate Range, yield 40Ar/39Ar ages of 12.1–14 Ma (Wagner and Hsu, 1988; Luckow et al., 2005; Andrew and Walker, 2009).

title: pyroclastic
description: This unit is a conspicuous white tuffaceous bed within the otherwise dark-colored basaltic-andesite lava flow sequence interbedded in the Miocene volcanic section in Anvil Spring Canyon. The exposures in Warm Spring and Anvil Canyons are generally reworked tuffaceous deposits.

title: biotite gneiss complex
description: Alternating and complex relationships of dark-colored biotite paragneiss and quartzofeldspathic orthogneiss in Surprise Canyon. This unit is locally intruded by a quartz monzonitic rock, see also the Mesoproterozoic quartz monzonite unit described above. Labotka et al. (1980) interpret a felsic volcanic rock as protolith to the quartz-microcline-plagioclase-muscovite gneiss.

title: allochthonous basement gneisses
description: A package of steeply dipping, well-foliated and strongly metamorphosed gneisses is only exposed in one small area of western Middle Park Canyon structurally and stratigraphically below the Crystal Springs Formation but still in the hanging wall of the Goldbug thrust. Much of the exposure of this unit is a layered gneiss of quart-feldspar light bands alternating with hornblende-rich dark layers. The layering occurs on a millimeter scale and is locally intruded by chocolate bar-style boudinaged, fine-grained amphibolitic sills. Other sections of this basement unit are massive amphibolitic gneisses also intruded by boundinaged mafic sills. These steeply dipping are overlain by a section of less metamorphosed, layered quartz-feldspar gneiss correlated to the Crystal Spring Formation. This contact is interpreted to be a nonconformity of the feldspathic quartzite member of Crystal Spring Formation deposited on the erosionally beveled older gneiss.

title: World beater complex in Warm SPring Canyon
description: Unit consists of gray, biotite-rich, quartz monzonitiic augen orthogneiss intruded by undeformed gray quartz monzonite (Lanphere et al., 1964). The augen are megacrysts of potassium feldspar up to 4 cm long. The gneiss contains inclusions of quartz-biotite-muscovite schist. The gneiss is intruded by undeformed, light gray equigranular to porphyritic quartz monzonite, crosscutting foliation and locally it is the dominant rock type. These two units are difficult to separate out and are thus mapped together as a unit. U-Pb zircon geochronology found ages for the gneiss and crosscutting intrusions of 1790 and 1350 Ma, respectively (Lanphere et al., 1964). Zircon U-Pb LA-ICPMS age of 1787.7 ± 1.6 Ma was obtained by Cobb (2015) from the same sample location as Lanphere et al. (1964).

title: mica schist
description: Biotite quartz-mica schist and associated metamorphic rocks (Wrucke et al., 2008) in northeastern Warm Spring Canyon are the oldest autochthonous units exposed in the map area. The igneous protolith of the Paleoproterozoic augen gneiss intruded the mica schist protolith and both were subsequently metamorphosed together.

title: World Beater complex
description: Unit consists of gray, biotite-rich, quartz monzonitiic augen orthogneiss intruded by undeformed gray quartz monzonite (Lanphere et al., 1964). The augen are megacrysts of potassium feldspar up to 4 cm long. The gneiss contains inclusions of quartz-biotite-muscovite schist. The gneiss is intruded by undeformed, light gray equigranular to porphyritic quartz monzonite, crosscutting foliation and locally it is the dominant rock type. These two units are difficult to separate out and are thus mapped together as a unit. U-Pb zircon geochronology found ages for the gneiss and crosscutting intrusions of 1790 and 1350 Ma, respectively (Lanphere et al., 1964). Zircon U-Pb LA-ICPMS age of 1787.7 ± 1.6 Ma was obtained by Cobb (2015) from the same sample location as Lanphere et al. (1964).

title: Beck Spring Dolomite
description: Blue-gray sandy dolomite with massive bedding and oolites. The thickness varies from 300 m thick to absent at the erosional unconformity with the overlying Kingston Peak Formation. Thinly laminated textures occur near the top.

title: Beck Spring Dolomite, quartzite
description: Light yellow-gray and pale-red colored, feldspathic quartzite with minor amounts of conglomerate and dolomite (Wrucke, 1966). Commonly 20–30% feldspar grains. The lower two-thirds are medium coarse-grained, in ~60 cm thick beds, while the upper third is fine to medium-grained in beds ~30 cm thick. Cross-bedding is common in the lower part and ripple marks are common in the upper part. Thin (~3 cm thick) lenses of conglomerate occur in the lower 20 m. A pebble to cobble conglomerate in coarse-grained quartzose matrix is locally present along the basal contact. The pebbles are mostly milky quartz, but schist and granitic pebbles are locally abundant. Near the top there are lenses of brown dolomite averaging 9 cm thick and 100 cm long. This unit is 190 m thick in the less deformed eastern Panamint Range.

title: Crystal Spring Formation, argillite member
description: Fine-grained, dark grayish purple to dark reddish-brown argillite in the lower two thirds with thin bedded siltite, silty argillite and minor dolomite in the upper third (Wrucke, 1966). Lighter color reduction spots are common in the lower unit. The undeformed thickness is about 80 m in the eastern Panamint Range.

title: Crystal Spring Formation, carbonate members
description: Combination of the two dolomite members of Wrucke (1966). The stromatolitic dolomite member is brownish-red, medium-grained dolomite with abundant stromatolites with interbedded brown-weathering sandy dolomite in the upper 25% of themember (Wrucke, 1966). Bedding is obscure, 1–10 m thick. Prominent cliff-former. The other member is a cherty dolomite: dominantly interbedded pale grayish-orange dolomite and brown to black chert, with lesser brown-weathering silty dolomite (Wrucke, 1966). The combined thickness is about 150 m where it is well exposed and relatively undeformed in the eastern Panamint Range.

title: Crystal Spring Formation, feldspathic quartzite member
description: Light yellow-gray and pale-red colored, feldspathic quartzite with minor amounts of conglomerate and dolomite (Wrucke, 1966). Commonly 20–30% feldspar grains. The lower two-thirds are medium coarse-grained, in ~60 cm thick beds, while the upper third is fine to medium-grained in beds ~30 cm thick. Cross-bedding is common in the lower part and ripple marks are common in the upper part. Thin (~3 cm thick) lenses of conglomerate occur in the lower 20 m. A pebble to cobble conglomerate in coarse-grained quartzose matrix is locally present along the basal contact. The pebbles are mostly milky quartz, but schist and granitic pebbles are locally abundant. Near the top there are lenses of brown dolomite averaging 9 cm thick and 100 cm long. This unit is 190 m thick in the less deformed eastern Panamint Range.

title: Crystal Spring Formation, siltite member
description: Finely laminated, very fine-grained, greenish- or purplish-black siltite with local thin beds of cream-gray chert (Wrucke, 1966). Small (<5 cm long) lenses of dolomite occur in the lower portion of this member. The base of this member is an unconformity (Wrucke, 1966). This unit is ~100 m- thick in the eastern Panamint Range.

title: Crystal Spring Formation, siltite member
description: Finely laminated, very fine-grained, greenish- or purplish-black siltite with local thin beds of cream-gray chert (Wrucke, 1966). Small (<5 cm long) lenses of dolomite occur in the lower portion of this member. The base of this member is an unconformity (Wrucke, 1966). This unit is ~100 m- thick in the eastern Panamint Range.

title: Crystal Spring Formation, diabase
description: Sills and dikes of metamorphosed mafic intrusive rocks that intrude the Crystal Spring Formation and older metamorphic rocks. This rock is typically dark colored and often characterized by ophitic intergrowth of plagioclase and pyroxene. These sills in the Kingston Range that are dated at 1087 Ma (Heaman and Grotzinger, 1992).

title: monzogranite
description: Undeformed or weakly deformed leuco-monzogranite intruded into Paleoproterozoic gneiss below Crystal Spring Formation in Surprise Canyon. This granite may correlate to Jurassic leucogranites elsewhere in Surprise Canyon because the poorly exposed intrusive relationships are difficult to interpret.

title: Johnnie Formation, lower member
description: Thick bedded dolomite and sandy dolomite interbedded with quartzite and dolomitic quartzite and overlain by dark-reddish-brown-weathering quartzite and pelite (Albee et al., 1981). 150–330 m thick (Labotka et al., 1980)

title: Johnnie Formation, middle member
description: Informal member of thin-bedded dolomitic marbles with reddish weathering. This is the upper part of the lower memebr of Labotka et al. (1980). About 45 m thick. Zjl

title: Johnnie Formation, upper member
description: Thinly laminated micaceous green argillite with rare sandy dolomite and limestone layers changing upward into gray argillite and gray-green silty limestone. Quartzite beds increase near the top. This member is 400–650 m thick (Labotka et al., 1980).

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Limekiln Spring Member, argillitic submember
description: Dark colored fine-grained meta-greywacke with lesser amounts of amphibolitic schist, and pelitic schist, and dolomite. Conglomerate, breccia and olistostromes layers are unevenly distributed within this unit in western exposures or Surprise and Happy Canyons, but not east of the main anticline of basement-Crystal Spring Formation and Beck Spring Dolomite. Dolomite-clast breccia layers are unevenly distributed within this unit. Granite-clast conglomerate occurs in great abundance in the region between Happy and Surprise Canyons with some clasts of granitic rock are several meters across.

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Limekiln Spring Member, argillitic submember
description: [Ed. not described on the map, assuming the same as Zkla] Dark colored fine-grained meta-greywacke with lesser amounts of amphibolitic schist, and pelitic schist, and dolomite. Conglomerate, breccia and olistostromes layers are unevenly distributed within this unit in western exposures or Surprise and Happy Canyons, but not east of the main anticline of basement-Crystal Spring Formation and Beck Spring Dolomite. Dolomite-clast breccia layers are unevenly distributed within this unit. Granite-clast conglomerate occurs in great abundance in the region between Happy and Surprise Canyons with some clasts of granitic rock are several meters across.

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Limekiln Spring Member
description: Heterogenous package of rocks, 50–500 m thick dominated by fine-grained metagraywacke, pelitic schist, and amphibolitic schist. Conglomeratic layers are locally abundant and contain clasts of Proterozoic basement or Beck Spring Dolomite. Several large olistostromes of Beck Spring Dolomite are exposed in this member in a syncline in Surprise Canyon.

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Limekiln Spring Member, quartzite submember
description: 140 m of light tan bedded quartzite and calcareous quartzite. Beds range from thin- to medium-bedded (Labotka et al., 1980).

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Limekiln Spring Member, breccia submember
description: Conglomerate and breccia of clasts and cobbles of underlying basement gneiss, Crystal Spring Formation and Beck Spring Dolomite. The boundary between this and several of the olistostromes along the Happy-Surprise divide is difficult to determine.

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Mountain Girl Member
description: Clast-supported arkosic sandstone with numerous white quartzose pebble to cobble sized clasts and minor limestone clasts. The lower part is dark-reddish to black weathering and more pebbly; the upper part is white weathering, less pebbly and more sandy. Most clasts are <10 cm in diameter. Promoted to member status from submember by Petterson et al. (2011). Locally in the cores of folds along the western Panamint Range, this unit is strongly deformed into stretched pebble conglomerate with 10:2:1 triaxial ellipsoid pebbles.

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Middle Park Member
description: This unit in the southern Panamint Range is a pervasively laminated schistose siltstone and sandstone. Farther to the north Petterson et al. (2011) describe a lower portion containing a few Sourdough Member-like limestones and a middle portion containing graywackes with medium to coarse-grained, predominantly quartz pebbles. Promoted to member status by Petterson et al. (2011).

title: Kingston Peak Formation, olistostrome
description: Local zones within many of the fine clastic units of the Kingston Peak Formation that are matrix-supported breccias of boulder to very large blocks of older rock units. Theses clasts are dominantly of the Crystal Spring Formation in Redlands Canyon but are mostly Beck Spring Dolomite farther north in Warm Spring, Happy, and Surprise Canyons. The matrix is typically fine-grained, dark gray-green to brown and is locally finely recrystallized due to thermal metamorphism from nearby plutonic rocks. These deposits probably represent rock avalanche deposits caused by syn-depositional normal faulting (Prave, 1999). Olistostromes large enough to map occur in the Limekiln Spring, Surprise, and Middle Park Members. Large olistostromes >280 m long occur in the Warm Spring Canyon area that were previously interpreted to be horses along thrust faults (Wrucke et al., 2008). Olistostromes in the Limekiln Spring Member are spectacularly exposed along the ridge between Happy and Surprise Canyons, where the exposed olistostromes appear to peel off from the depositional source outcrops of the Beck Spring Dolomite and become clasts in fine -grained argillite matrix.

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Surprise Member
description: Thick section (250–1000 m) of clastic rocks, massive to unbedded trimodal to unsorted pebbly mudstone and diamictite. The clasts are generally smaller than 10 cm in diameter, but clasts of several meters occur locally. Clast rock types include: quartzo-feldspathic gneiss, quartzite, dolomite, argillite, and diabase. Graded argillite beds with exotic cobbles also occur in the member. A basalt layer occurs near the middle of this member (Johnson, 1957; Albee et al., 1981).

title: Kingston Peak Formation, basalt flow layer within the Surprise Member
description: Typically exposed as a massive, fine-grained, dark gray to black colored meta-volcanic rock. Where well-exposed farther north in South Park, Pleasant, and Happy Canyons there are abundant well-preserved pillow structures, basal flow breccia, hyaloclastic textures and white amygdules. A spectacular exposure of deformed pillows occurs south of the mouth of Happy Canyon, where pillows become 10:2:1 triaxial ellipsoids.

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Sourdough Limestone
description: Thin, variable thickness (5–30 m) thinly laminated light- and dark-gray micaceous limestone (Johnson, 1957; Albee, et al., 1981). Thickness varies due to imbrications and stratigraphic omission from Mesozoic and Neogene contractional and extensional deformation. A well-exposed section in Big Horn Canyon has three complete thrust duplications of this member along with the overlying Middle Park Member. 36°07’30” N

title: Kingston Peak Formation, South Park Member
Kingston Peak Formation, Thorndike Member
description: Buff to tan-colored limestone, with strong variability, formally defined by Petterson et al. (2011). Dominantly well-laminated limestone with siliceous irregular beds or argillite. There are also local, thick massive light-colored limestone beds and lenses. The unit varies in thickness from a meter to several meters thick. Many of these exposures were previously mapped by other workers as out of place Sourdough Limestone Member.

title: Kingston Peak Formation, Wildrose Diamictite
description: Diamictite of very dark brownweathering fine-grained matrix with abundant clasts of limestone, quartzite, granitic, and gneiss. This unit is only locally present but occurs throughout the Panamint Range. Generally, there are more abundant basement gneiss and quartzite clasts, but certain areas contain numerous clasts of massive bluish gray dolomite correlated to the Beck Spring Dolomite. Clast size is usually pebble to cobble sized but boulder clasts up to 3 m do occur locally (Miller, 1987). Promoted to member status by Petterson et al. (2011).

title: Noonday Dolomite
description: Dominantly dolomite and dolomitic limestone, extensively metamorphosed adjacent to the Manly Peak quartz monzonite. Exposures on the western range flank are locally strongly brecciated and displaced down slope by extensional faulting or mass wasting. These rocks weather to a distinctive light-yellow color visible from a distance. Age interpreted from Macdonald et al. (2013).

title: Noonday Dolomite
description: Dominantly dolomite and dolomitic limestone, extensively metamorphosed adjacent to the Manly Peak quartz monzonite. Exposures on the western range flank are locally strongly brecciated and displaced down slope by extensional faulting or mass wasting. These rocks weather to a distinctive light-yellow color visible from a distance. Age interpreted from Macdonald et al. (2013).

title: Noonday Dolomite, Mahagony Flat Member
description: 125–150 m of thick-bedded to massive light-gray dolomite with minor thin argillite beds near the top. This unit was originally mapped in the map area as the Redlands Member by Johnson (1957) but renamed and redefined by Petterson et al. (2011).

title: Noonday Dolomite, Radclif Member
description: 100–250 m of thin-bedded gray, pink, green, or brown limestone interbedded with thin laminae of gray-green argillaceous limestones and argillites. Lower part consists almost entirely of argillite but includes lenses of conglomerate containing clasts of argillite and dolomite in argillaceous dolomite matrix (Albee et al., 1981).

title: Noonday Dolomite, Sentinel Peak Member
description: Variable thickness (3–150 m) due to faulting, light-gray massive dolomite containing thinly laminated siliceous limestone in lower part. Thin laminae and tubular structures are common (Albee et al., 1981). The tube structures are oriented normal to the bedding and are composed of coarser grained calcite. title: Stirling Quartzite
description: Brown-weathering quartzite at top, underlain by interbedded purple shale and quartzite and at the base it is well-bedded and cross-bedded partly conglomeratic quartzite (Hunt and Mabey, 1966).
